lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Chapter title. Leave a clean beat before story begins.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The desert didn't end so much as it thinned.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: By late afternoon the dunes had flattened into hard, broken ground scattered with the first signs of people who lived too close to nothing: a collapsed sheepfold, a half-buried boundary stone, a scatter of broken pottery no one had bothered to gather. The air carried the faint greasy smell of cooking fires and the sharper edge of river mud. Uruk was still hours away, but the land had started remembering it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They walked in a loose line. BAH-lahg kept the donkeys moving with short clicks of his tongue. En-HEH-doo had fallen a few paces back. Zeek stayed near the middle, the journal still in the pack where he'd left it the day before.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: A low mud-brick wall appeared on the right, half-swallowed by sand. Someone had tried to keep a garden once. A few dried stalks still clung to the soil like they hadn't gotten the message. BAH-lahg stopped the animals and walked the length of the wall, testing the corners with the heel of his boot.

lines.speaker: Balag
lines.text: Someone put real work into this,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Balag
lines.text: Foundations are deeper than they needed to be.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek came up beside him. He ran a hand along the top course. The mortar was ordinary, but the joints had been laid with care. Whoever built it had known what they were doing and still lost the argument with the desert.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: One section near the middle had slumped. Two courses of brick had shifted outward, the mortar cracked into a long jagged seam. It wasn't dangerous. It also wasn't right.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek set his pack down, pulled the bronze awl and a short length of cord from the side pocket, and began working without asking anyone's opinion. He scraped the loose mortar free, tapped the shifted bricks back into true, then bound the seam with the cord driven through fresh holes so the load would sit properly again. It wouldn't last another season. It would last longer than it would have if he'd walked past it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: BAH-lahg watched for a while, then said,
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: BAH-lahg stood beside him a while longer.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek packed fresh mortar into the seam with his thumb.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: The people who built this wall are gone.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: They spent days making sure it stood.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: So somebody should respect the effort.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek looked along the crumbling length of brick disappearing into the sand.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: The next person who leans against it.

lines.speaker: Balag
lines.text: You fix things you'll never see again.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: I excavate things no one remembers.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: En-HEH-doo brushed dust from her knees and joined them.

lines.speaker: Enhedu
lines.text: He'd spend weeks fixing channels on land that wasn't his.

lines.speaker: Enhedu
lines.text: He said the water couldn't read ownership marks.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The sound surprised all three of them.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: BAH-lahg looked from one to the other.

lines.speaker: Balag
lines.text: I preferred it when neither of you talked.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: En-HEH-doo rested a hand on the repaired section of wall.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The three of them stood looking at the wall for another moment.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The new cord crossed the old brick in pale lines that anyone could see.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Someone else would come along one day and know another pair of hands had cared enough to keep it standing a little longer.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: That was all. He finished the last knot, tested the repaired section with his weight, and stood. The wall still leaned a little. It no longer looked like it was giving up.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: En-HEH-doo had wandered over during the work. She crouched, picked up one of the loose bricks Zeek had set aside, weighed it in her hand, then set it neatly back into the gap he hadn't needed. No comment. Just the brick returned to where it belonged.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They didn't rest long after that. The light was already sliding toward the kind of copper dusk that made distances hard to trust. Zeek adjusted a slipped pack strap on the nearer donkey while the others drank. The motion was automatic. His hands knew the work even when his mind was somewhere else.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: BAH-lahg watched him a moment longer than necessary.

lines.speaker: Balag
lines.text: You still thinking about the Collector?

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: I'm thinking about what I'm not going to tell him.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: BAH-lahg gave a short nod, as if that answer was the only one he'd expected.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They started walking again. The broken ground gradually gave way to the first real tracks—cart ruts, donkey dung, the scuffed places where people had stood arguing about tolls or water or nothing important at all. The smell of the city grew stronger. Smoke. Onions. The particular sourness of too many bodies living too close together.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek felt the mark under the linen give a single slow pulse. Not a demand. Just a reminder that it was still there.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Ahead, the first low roofs of the outer districts hunched against the darkening sky.
